name: Modifying a List (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that increments all values of the list by 1.
code:
#Step 1: Define and initialize the list
lst = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
#Step 2: Iterate through the list elements 
for i in range(len(lst)):
    #Step 2.1: Increment the element at index i by 1
    lst[i] += 1
#Step 3: Print the list
print(lst)

commentList: This line creates a list of numbers and stores it in the variable lst so you have the values you'll later increment.
Syntax: lst = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] uses square brackets to make a list and = to assign it; you must separate items with commas.
Be careful: if the list contains non-numeric values (for example strings), then doing lst[i] += 1 later will raise an error, so you should ensure the items are numbers.
Don't confuse square brackets [] with parentheses (). If you use parentheses (or omit brackets incorrectly) you may create a different type that you cannot modify the same way.
Best practice: choose a clearer variable name than lst (for example numbers) to make your code easier to read, and if you need to keep the original list unchanged, make a copy before modifying it.
Alternative approach: if you need a sequence of consecutive numbers, you can create it with list(range(1, 7)) so you don't have to type every element manually.

commentList: Purpose: This line starts a loop that visits every index of lst so you can update each element in place; you need the index because you will assign back to lst[i].
Syntax breakdown: 'for' begins the loop, 'i' is the loop variable, 'range(len(lst))' produces integers 0 through len(lst)-1, and the trailing ':' starts the indented block that runs for each i.
What it does step-by-step: len(lst) gives the number of items, range(...) creates a sequence of valid indices, and on each loop iteration i takes the next index value so you can access lst[i].

Common mistakes: If you write 'for x in lst:' and then do 'x += 1' you will not change the original list elements because x is a separate value; using indices (as here) lets you modify the list itself.

Edge cases and errors: If you forget the ':' or misindent the following line you'll get a SyntaxError; if you insert or remove items from lst while using range(len(lst)) you can get unexpected behavior because the indices were based on the original length.

Best practice suggestions: If you also need the current value, consider 'for i, val in enumerate(lst): lst[i] = val + 1' for clarity, or use a list comprehension 'lst = [x + 1 for x in lst]' for a more Pythonic and often clearer solution.

commentList: This line updates the current list element so you add 1 to the value at index i, which is how the program increments every item in the list.
Here lst[i] selects the element at position i and the += operator means "add 1 and store the result back"; in other words it's equivalent to lst[i] = lst[i] + 1, so you modify the list in place.

Be aware of common mistakes: if you wrote i += 1 you would change the loop index instead of the list element; if i were outside the valid range you'd get an IndexError (though using range(len(lst)) prevents that), and if an element is not a number you'll get a TypeError when you try to add 1.

If you want clearer code you can use enumerate to get both index and value (for i, val in enumerate(lst): lst[i] = val + 1), or use a list comprehension (lst = [x + 1 for x in lst]) if you prefer creating a new list instead of changing the original.
For good habits, use descriptive names (e.g., values instead of lst) and choose in-place modification or creating a new list deliberately so you don't accidentally change data you need elsewhere.

commentList: You use this line to display the list after incrementation so you can verify the program changed every element.
print(lst) calls the print function with lst as its argument; you pass the variable name and Python shows the list with brackets and commas (e.g., [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]).

If you forget to define lst before this line you'll get a NameError; also, don't put quotes around lst (print('lst')) unless you want to print the literal text 'lst', and don't write lst() because that tries to call the list as a function.

If you modified a copy instead of lst (for example by creating a new list and not assigning it back), you may see unchanged values when you print; make sure you updated the lst variable itself (e.g., lst[i] += 1).

As a best practice, you can make the output clearer by adding a label like print('Updated list:', lst), and if you need the value for later use or testing, consider returning lst from a function instead of printing it.

distractors.description: Step-by-step why you might pick this: you see a loop and assume the loop variable i will let you access each position to change the list. It looks shorter and simpler, so you pick it. What actually happens: with this line i becomes each element value (1, then 2, etc.), not an index. If the following code still tries to use i as an index (for example, doing lst[i] += 1), you will try to access positions 1, 2, ... 6 — and when you reach a value that is outside the list bounds you'll get an IndexError. If instead you tried to do i += 1 inside the loop, that just changes the local variable i and does not modify the list element. Why this is wrong for the task: you need a way to update elements inside the list by position, but this line makes i hold values, not positions, so you cannot reliably assign the incremented value back into the list. The key missing idea is that you must obtain or use the element's index when you want to write the incremented value back into the list.

Why you might choose this: if you naturally count starting at 1, you might write the loop to start at 1 and expect to touch every element. What actually happens: this loop starts at index 1 and goes up to index len(lst)-1. That means index 0 (the first element) is never visited, so the first element will not be incremented. The rest of the elements will be updated, so the bug can be subtle — your output will show most values changed but the first unchanged — which makes this a tempting but incorrect choice. The underlying misconception is zero-based indexing; the result is a skipped element rather than a runtime error, which can be harder to notice during quick checks.

You might choose this because you think increasing the index variable i will somehow increase the element it refers to. Step by step: this line increments the loop variable i, not any value inside the list. In a for-loop that uses range(...), the loop assigns a new i at the start of each iteration, so your manual change is overwritten on the next iteration — the list elements remain unchanged. Using this distractor will not raise an error, but it will fail to modify the list values; the program will still run but the output will not reflect incremented elements. This is wrong because it targets the index rather than the stored value at that index; it misunderstands which variable holds the data you need to change.
